questions.q: What infrastructure hop does Zerobus Ingest eliminate compared to the traditional pattern?
options: The message bus (e.g. Kafka) and the separate Spark Structured Streaming job that reads from it — producers write directly to a Delta table instead
Unity Catalog governance, since Zerobus bypasses GRANT-based permissions entirely
The Delta table itself, since Zerobus writes to a proprietary format
The producing application, since Zerobus generates synthetic data automatically
questions.explain: Zerobus lets a producer push event data directly into a Delta table, removing the message-bus-plus-streaming-job hop that was pure overhead when the lakehouse is the only destination.

questions.q: Per Zerobus's published specifications, what is the near real-time ingestion latency and the max throughput per client?
options: Under 5 seconds latency, up to 100 MB/sec per client
Under 5 milliseconds latency, up to 1 GB/sec per client
Under 5 minutes latency, up to 10 MB/sec per client
Latency and throughput are not published anywhere
questions.explain: Zerobus's published specs are near real-time ingestion under 5 seconds and up to 100 MB/sec throughput per client, with thousands of concurrent clients supported per table.

questions.q: A team needs Change Data Feed on data written by Zerobus Ingest, so they can sync inserts/updates/deletes downstream. What does this lesson say is the current real limitation and workaround?
options: Zerobus does not natively support CDF on its target table; the workaround is to stream that table into a second table with CDF enabled
Zerobus fully supports CDF natively with no workaround needed
CDF is only available if the target table uses JSON instead of Delta format
Change Data Feed is being deprecated platform-wide, so this is a non-issue
questions.explain: As of this writing, Zerobus does not support CDF directly on the table it writes to — the documented workaround streams that table into a second, CDF-enabled table.

questions.q: In the NEOWISE benchmark, what real, published result did Zerobus Ingest achieve, and on what kind of dataset?
options: 1 petabyte in 24 hours, 12 GB/s sustained, 12 million rows per second, on real NASA telescope data chosen because it behaves like production telemetry
1 gigabyte in 24 hours on a synthetic load generator
1 petabyte in 24 hours, but only achievable with Kafka in front of Zerobus
The benchmark used fabricated data with no real-world basis
questions.explain: Databricks deliberately chose NASA's real NEOWISE dataset (200 billion time-stamped detections) because it behaves like production telemetry, and the benchmark reached 1PB/24hr, 12GB/s sustained, 12M rows/sec, with zero pre-configuration.

questions.q: What does Zerobus's 'dynamic partitioning' engineering bet actually guarantee, per this lesson?
options: Ordering is guaranteed at the stream connection level rather than the partition level, enabling pods to be added or removed dynamically for true elastic autoscaling
Every message is partitioned alphabetically by field name
Partitions are fixed at stream creation and can never change afterward
Partitioning is handled entirely by the client application, not by Zerobus
questions.explain: By guaranteeing order at the connection level instead of a fixed partition level, Zerobus can scale pods up and down dynamically — true elastic autoscaling rather than scale-out bound to a pre-set partition count.
